narrative:
# Weekly Multi-Asset Technology & Growth Market Briefing

The past week delivered a sharp and disorderly factor rotation across our growth and technology universe, with pronounced drawdowns in software, cybersecurity, and select semiconductor names offset by renewed strength in energy, materials, and a handful of idiosyncratic winners. Price action was dominated far more by positioning, factor unwinds, and cross-asset de-risking than by name-specific fundamentals, as evidenced by the broad, correlated selloff in high-multiple software and applied AI, alongside notable resilience in cash-generative cyclicals and select capital-intensive stories. Against this backdrop, our watchlist showed extreme dispersion: Braze (BRZE) rallied 25.5% over the week, while Coinbase (COIN) fell 18.4%, Micron (MU) declined 15.5%, and multiple cybersecurity and data-platform names sold off more than 10%, underscoring the need to separate cyclical and positioning-driven weakness from genuine thesis impairment. With no near-term earnings catalysts on deck for our coverage over the next two weeks, next week’s playbook is primarily about risk management, sizing, and opportunistic rotation rather than binary event risk.

## Market Overview

This week’s tape in our watchlist was characterized by a broad de-risking of growth, particularly in software infrastructure, application software, cybersecurity, and certain semiconductor exposures, with drawdowns in the high single to mid-teens across many of the most crowded winners of the past twelve months. Within software infrastructure, Meta Platforms (META) declined 11.4% on the week, alongside UiPath (PATH) at minus 11.4%, Fair Isaac (FICO) at minus 10.3%, Samsara (IOT) at minus 10.2%, MongoDB (MDB) at minus 9.8%, Snowflake (SNOW) at minus 9.1%, and Elastic (ESTC) at minus 9.0%. The primary outlier was Fastly (FSLY), which rallied 8.8% over the week despite the broader growth selloff, highlighting the importance of idiosyncratic catalysts, short-covering, and factor exposures even within a seemingly homogenous bucket.

Application software showed similarly heavy pressure, consistent with a factor rotation away from high-duration, high-multiple names that had benefitted from the AI-adjacent narrative and benign rate expectations. Within this cohort, Hims & Hers (HIMS) fell 12.0%, Atlassian (TEAM) declined 11.7%, ServiceTitan (TTAN) and HubSpot (HUBS) each declined 10.8%, monday.com (MNDY) fell 10.0%, ServiceNow (NOW) declined 9.9%, Workday (WDAY) dropped 8.7%, and Intuit (INTU) was down 8.6% over the week. The breadth and depth of this move, in the absence of company-specific catalysts, speaks to a macro and positioning-driven de-risking, rather than a discrete shift in the earnings outlook for any single name.

Cybersecurity equities were among the most aggressively sold segments of the week, reversing a multi-quarter period of outperformance and rich multiple expansion. Tenable (TENB) declined 16.6% and Rapid7 (RPD) fell 16.5% over the week, with Zscaler (ZS) down 12.1%, SentinelOne (S) and Qualys (QLYS) each down 11.2%, Varonis (VRNS) down 10.6%, Palo Alto Networks (PANW) down 9.8%, and CrowdStrike (CRWD) down 9.6%. This synchronous decline in leaders, challengers, and turnaround stories suggests that investors were reducing sector exposure broadly rather than discriminating on fundamentals, which may create opportunities to add to higher-quality franchises with durable growth, expanding free cash flow, and potential AI tailwinds.

Semiconductors and related design and IP names experienced material volatility, but with more pronounced dispersion than in software, reflecting differing exposures to memory, AI compute, custom silicon, and optical interconnect. Micron (MU), a bellwether for memory and storage cycles, fell 15.5% on the week and 16.7% over the past month, while SanDisk (SNDK) declined 13.2% and POET Technologies (POET) fell 12.5%. Quantum computing player IonQ (IONQ) declined 11.8%, and Synopsys (SNPS) was down 9.5%, while Credo (CRDO) declined 7.9%. In sharp contrast, Arm Holdings (ARM) gained 8.9% and Marvell (MRVL) advanced 7.9%, underscoring investor preference for perceived AI-enablers with asset-light, IP-centric models and structural content growth.

Outside of pure technology, adtech, fintech, consumer, and energy/industrials painted a more nuanced picture of risk appetite and macro sentiment. In AdTech and digital media, Braze (BRZE) surged 25.5% for the week and 30.8% over the month, while Zeta Global (ZETA) fell 14.2%, AppLovin (APP) declined 13.8%, and The Trade Desk (TTD) fell 11.7%. In fintech, Coinbase (COIN) was the notable laggard, down 18.4% on the week and 12.4% on the month, while Shift4 Payments (FOUR) gained 8.0%, and Block (XYZ) was down a more modest 5.7%. Consumer-facing names were mixed, with Global-E (GLBE) down 10.5% and GoDaddy (GDDY) down 5.8%, while PVH (PVH) gained 5.0% and Mondelez (MDLZ) advanced 3.7%. Energy and industrials were a relative bright spot, with Sable Offshore (SOC) up 13.3% on the week and an exceptional 102.1% on the month, Corning (GLW) up 9.8%, CF Industries (CF) up 9.2%, Eastman Chemical (EMN) up 9.0%, California Resources (CRC) up 8.3%, Agnico Eagle (AEM) and Freeport-McMoRan (FCX) each up 8.0%, and CNH Industrial (CNH) up 7.8%.

The net effect across the watchlist is a classic risk-off rotation, with capital flowing out of unprofitable or long-duration growth, particularly in software and select AI stories, and into cash-generative cyclicals and more tangible asset stories in energy, materials, and industrials. With no watchlist earnings scheduled over the next two weeks, the near-term path of returns will be dictated by macro data, rate expectations, and positioning adjustments rather than company-specific prints, which tends to amplify factor volatility. For portfolio construction, the week reinforced the value of diversified factor exposures, the importance of valuation discipline even in high-quality compounders, and the need for a nimble approach to AI-related narratives that can swing sentiment sharply without corresponding changes in fundamentals.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

Sector leadership this week was clearly anchored in energy, materials, and selected industrial exposures, while prior leaders in software, cybersecurity, and AI-adjacent themes lagged. Within our energy and industrials bucket, Sable Offshore (SOC) stood out with a 13.3% gain for the week and a remarkable 102.1% gain over the month, pointing to a combination of idiosyncratic drivers, increased investor interest in offshore development, and possibly short-covering in a name that had been relatively under-owned. Corning (GLW) gained 9.8% during the week, even as it remained down 14.7% for the month, suggesting a rebound from oversold conditions and growing investor appreciation for its leverage to datacenter, display, and optical connectivity themes within the broader AI infrastructure build-out. CF Industries added 9.2% for the week and 41.9% for the month, making it one of the strongest performers across our watchlist on a trailing-month basis, consistent with tightening nitrogen markets and renewed interest in agricultural inputs.

Materials and commodity-exposed names beyond CF also reasserted leadership. Eastman Chemical (EMN) rose 9.0% on the week despite being down 5.7% for the month, while gold and copper proxies like Agnico Eagle (AEM) and Freeport-McMoRan (FCX) each gained 8.0% after experiencing 1-month drawdowns of 19.6% and 18.3%, respectively. Mosaic (MOS) gained 6.0% for the week but remained down 7.3% on the month, highlighting how sector-level interest in commodities can lift even laggard names once positioning becomes sufficiently washed out. Kaiser Aluminum (KALU) rose 7.0% this week but is still down 13.3% over the month, reinforcing the idea that some of this week’s cyclicals strength may be more about mean reversion and short-covering than a full-blown re-rating of global demand expectations.

Within energy producers, we observed robust performance across both integrated and exploration-focused stories, consistent with a market that remains concerned about supply discipline, geopolitical risk, and the resilience of demand. Occidental Petroleum (OXY) gained 7.6% this week and 28.2% over the prior month, while Devon Energy (DVN) gained 7.0% on the week and 22.2% on the month. Downstream, Valero (VLO) added 6.0% for the week and an impressive 27.4% on the month, emphasizing how refining margins and capital returns remain a powerful draw for investors looking for real cash flow and shareholder yield in a volatile macro environment. California Resources (CRC) gained 8.3% for the week and 18.5% over the month, marking it as another beneficiary of investor interest in leveraged energy beta and regional supply dynamics.

By contrast, software as a broad factor underperformed meaningfully, as captured by the iShares IGV software ETF, which was down 7.3% for the week and 4.9% for the month. The ETF’s decline mirrors the drawdowns we see in our individual holdings across infrastructure, application, and vertical software. Infrastructure-facing names like Meta (META) at minus 11.4%, UiPath (PATH) at minus 11.4%, and MongoDB (MDB) at minus 9.8% gave up a material portion of prior gains, while application players such as HIMS at minus 12.0%, Atlassian at minus 11.7%, and ServiceNow at minus 9.9% also came under pressure. Vertical and industrial software names, including Bentley Systems (BSY) at minus 8.2%, PTC (PTC) at minus 8.1%, Procore (PCOR) at minus 6.6%, and Constellation Software (CSU.TO) at minus 5.6%, similarly traded lower, underlining that the de-rating pressure is broad-based and not limited to a single subsector.

Cybersecurity, previously a defensive growth pocket, saw one of the most aggressive de-ratings, reflecting both a crowded long factor and some investor concern about pricing power, platform consolidation, and competition. Tenable (TENB) and Rapid7 (RPD) each fell over 16% on the week, while Zscaler (ZS), SentinelOne (S), Qualys (QLYS), Varonis (VRNS), Palo Alto Networks (PANW), and CrowdStrike (CRWD) all experienced weekly drawdowns ranging from approximately 9% to 12%. Check Point (CHKP) declined 9.1% and Rubrik (RBRK) fell 7.2%, indicating that both established incumbents and newer challengers were subject to the same risk-off dynamics. From a rotation standpoint, we interpret this not as a rejection of the long-term cybersecurity thesis, but as a clearing-out of crowded positioning and a re-basing of valuation ahead of the next leg of demand driven by AI-era threats and regulatory pressures.

Semiconductors displayed a more nuanced leadership pattern, with weakness in memory and storage balanced by strength in AI-centered IP and connectivity. Micron (MU) declined 15.5%, SanDisk (SNDK) fell 13.2%, POET declined 12.5%, IonQ fell 11.8%, Synopsys dropped 9.5%, and Credo declined 7.9%, reflecting concerns about cyclical peaks, competitive intensity, and elevated expectations embedded in valuations. Conversely, Arm (ARM) and Marvell (MRVL) gained 8.9% and 7.9% respectively over the week, as investors gravitated toward perceived beneficiaries of AI compute proliferation, custom accelerators, and networked storage architectures. Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) also gained 5.1% this week and 36.5% for the month, suggesting renewed optimism around specialty foundry capacity, analog/mixed-signal content, and strategic optionality following prior deal-related volatility.

Adtech and digital media exhibited extremes of both outperformance and underperformance. Braze (BRZE) was a standout gainer at 25.5% for the week and 30.8% for the month, while Zeta (ZETA) declined 14.2%, AppLovin (APP) fell 13.8%, and The Trade Desk (TTD) dropped 11.7%. Pinterest (PINS) was a more modest laggard at minus 4.9%, and RAMP (LiveRamp) fell 3.2%, while Comcast (CMCSA) declined 2.4% and Netflix (NFLX) rose 1.8%. This dispersion hints at investors differentiating more finely between first-party data moats, exposure to brand versus performance advertising, and the ability to monetize incremental AI-driven personalization.

Fintech rotation dynamics were somewhat more muted but still indicative of a shift away from higher-beta exposures. Coinbase (COIN) was a major underperformer at minus 18.4% on the week and minus 12.4% on the month, likely reflective of risk-off sentiment in digital assets and ongoing regulatory and liquidity concerns. That said, Shift4 Payments (FOUR) gained 8.0% this week despite a 22.5% decline over the month, hinting at short covering or a reassessment of its end-market exposure. Bill Holdings (BILL) fell 7.2%, Block (XYZ) declined 5.7%, and Global Payments (GPN) fell 3.8%, while Capital One (COF) and Affirm (AFRM) declined 3.0% and 2.9% respectively. Morgan Stanley (MS) was a relative outperformer within the large-bank cohort, down only 1.9% on the week.

Finally, within consumer and service names, we saw a selective preference for defensives and quality growth over more speculative e-commerce plays. Global-E (GLBE) fell 10.5% and GoDaddy (GDDY) declined 5.8% for the week, while PVH (PVH) gained 5.0%, Mondelez (MDLZ) was up 3.7%, Unilever (UL) was down 3.4%, and GigaCloud (GCT) rose 3.2%. Healthcare services were also weak, with UnitedHealth (UNH) down 6.0% and broader healthcare under some pressure. The rotation ultimately favored hard-asset plays and cash generative businesses, while penalizing long-duration growth and more speculative AI narratives.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

One of the week’s most notable positive outliers was Braze (BRZE), which gained 25.5% over the week and 30.8% over the month, making it the strongest performer on our watchlist in the AdTech/MarTech cohort. While there were no major earnings releases from the watchlist in the last few days, Braze’s move appears driven by follow-through buying after a well-received prior earnings print and increasing investor conviction in customer engagement platforms with strong first-party data capabilities. The magnitude of the move, especially against a broadly risk-off software tape, suggests a combination of multiple expansion, fundamental buyers leaning in, and shorts covering. For portfolio positioning, the key question is whether the new valuation adequately reflects the multi-year growth runway in omnichannel and AI-driven customer engagement, or whether the stock has become more vulnerable to any deceleration in net new ARR or marketing budgets.

On the negative side, Coinbase (COIN) fell 18.4% over the week and 12.4% over the month, making it the worst-performing fintech name on our watchlist and one of the sharpest decliners overall. The move reflects both sector-specific headwinds in digital assets and broader factor pressures on high-beta growth. Investor attention remains focused on trading volumes, regulatory developments, and the sustainability of fee levels in a more competitive environment. The combination of macro risk-off and crypto-specific uncertainty tends to magnify volatility in COIN, and the magnitude of this week’s drawdown could present an opportunity for tactical traders, but longer-term allocations will likely remain cautious until there is greater clarity on regulatory and structural profitability.

Among cybersecurity names, Tenable (TENB) and Rapid7 (RPD) were the biggest negative movers, each declining 16.6% and 16.5% respectively. Both have historically been perceived as mid-cap, high-growth security names that can be more sensitive to valuation compression and shifts in security budget priorities. The drawdowns this week appear primarily factor-driven, given that larger peers such as Zscaler, SentinelOne, Qualys, Varonis, Palo Alto Networks, and CrowdStrike also saw sizable declines, though somewhat less severe than TENB and RPD. In the absence of incremental company-specific news, we interpret this as an indiscriminate selloff that may create opportunities to upgrade the quality mix within cybersecurity exposure, emphasizing platforms with stronger operating leverage, higher renewal visibility, and clearer AI-enhanced product roadmaps.

Micron (MU) exemplified the cyclical volatility of memory and storage, declining 15.5% on the week and 16.7% over the month. The move comes after a period in which Micron had been a key beneficiary of the AI data center build and the expectation of a memory upcycle, and the correction suggests investors are increasingly concerned about the sustainability of pricing, potential capacity additions, and the risk of a mid-cycle pause. Similar weakness in data storage peers like SanDisk (SNDK), down 13.2% on the week and 2.6% on the month, and Seagate (STX), down 7.6% on the week and 9.9% on the month, reinforces the notion that the market is reassessing the near-term risk-reward in storage and memory after a strong run. For long-term investors, the structural AI-driven demand story for high-bandwidth memory and advanced storage remains intact, but entry points and position sizing need to reflect the sector’s inherent cyclicality.

In the AI and data infrastructure complex, several names that had been strong beneficiaries of the AI narrative experienced meaningful pullbacks. MongoDB (MDB) declined 9.8% for the week and 25.2% for the month, C3.ai (AI) fell 8.4% for the week and 24.7% for the month, Elastic (ESTC) declined 9.0% for the week and 16.3% for the month, and GitLab (GTLB) fell 8.5% for the week and 21.6% for the month. These drawdowns reflect investor recalibration of the extent to which near-term AI monetization can justify elevated valuations, especially in the absence of near-term earnings catalysts. Datadog (DDOG), while also down 8.5% for the week, is still up 3.8% over the month, highlighting a somewhat more resilient investor perception around observability’s central role in managing AI-driven workloads.

The broader hyperscaler complex also saw meaningful weakness. Meta Platforms (META) declined 11.4% on the week and 19.6% on the month, Alphabet (GOOG) fell 8.4% on the week and 12.6% on the month, and Microsoft (MSFT) dropped 6.6% on the week and 10.9% on the month. While the fundamental AI investment and monetization cases for these companies remain strong, the recent pullbacks indicate that valuations had embedded a high degree of AI optimism, and that macro and rate jitters can quickly translate into multiple compression even for the highest-quality mega-caps. For long-only investors, this pullback provides a chance to reassess size and time horizon rather than reconsider the core thesis, which is still underpinned by durable cloud, advertising, productivity, and AI platform advantages.

In contrast to the risk-off tone in much of software and AI, some idiosyncratic winners emerged in hardware, networking, and specialty materials. Marvell (MRVL) gained 7.9% this week and 17.2% over the month, reflecting its positioning as a leveraged play on AI accelerators, custom ASICs, and networking silicon. Arm (ARM) added 8.9% this week and 9.4% on the month, as investors continued to embrace its royalty-based, asset-light model and its central role in low-power computing and custom silicon design for AI and edge devices. Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) advanced 5.1% this week and 36.5% for the month, capitalizing on expectations for robust demand for specialty foundry services. Corning (GLW), with its 9.8% weekly gain, remains down 14.7% over the month, but its performance this week signals investor recognition of its leverage to the AI hardware cycle through optical connectivity, specialty glass, and advanced materials.

In adtech and digital advertising, the dispersion between Braze and its peers was striking. Zeta Global (ZETA) fell 14.2% over the week and 18.5% over the month, AppLovin (APP) declined 13.8% on the week and 9.6% on the month, and The Trade Desk (TTD) fell 11.7% for the week and 15.4% for the month. LiveRamp (RAMP) and Pinterest (PINS) were modest laggards, down 3.2% and 4.9% respectively, while Netflix (NFLX) gained 1.8% on the week. The dispersion suggests that investors are differentiating more aggressively between business models exposed to mobile gaming, CTV, identity resolution, and omnichannel customer engagement, with Braze currently capturing a disproportionate share of incremental risk capital.

It is important to note that across our watchlist there were no earnings scheduled in the upcoming two weeks, which means that the week’s moves were largely disconnected from fresh earnings information. The absence of near-term earnings catalysts can increase sensitivity to macro headlines, rate moves, and factor flows, as investors lack company-specific news to anchor expectations. As a result, this week’s extremes—both positive and negative—should be interpreted through the lens of positioning and sentiment as much as fundamentals. The lack of imminent earnings also gives portfolio managers more flexibility to adjust exposures without needing to hold through binary events, which can further amplify short-term moves as risk is taken off or added quickly.

## Macro & Rates Environment

From a macro and rates perspective, the most defining feature of the current environment for our watchlist is uncertainty rather than any single data point or policy action. In recent sessions, markets have been grappling with unresolved questions around the trajectory of inflation, the durability of growth, and the timing and magnitude of any potential central bank easing. For high-duration growth assets—particularly unprofitable software, early-stage AI, and long-dated secular stories—this uncertainty manifests in heightened sensitivity to any perceived hawkish shift in rate expectations, even when the underlying data remain mixed. The pattern of the week’s moves across sectors is consistent with investors assigning a higher risk premium to long-duration cash flows while favoring nearer-term cash generators in energy, materials, and industrials.

The cross-asset setup has also been shaped by the dynamic interplay between inflation expectations and growth fears. When investors worry that inflation could remain sticky while growth decelerates, they tend to reduce exposure to the most valuation-sensitive, growth-oriented names, as we observed in our software and AI buckets. At the same time, real-economy cyclicals with tangible assets and near-term pricing power—such as energy producers, fertilizer companies, and industrials—can attract incremental capital as hedges against stagflation-like scenarios. The outperformance of CF Industries, Valero, Occidental, and Devon alongside the underperformance of names like ServiceNow, Atlassian, and MongoDB fits this pattern, reinforcing the idea that macro and rates narratives, even absent precise numbers, are currently favoring the value and cyclical side of the barbell.

Rate volatility remains a crucial driver of risk appetite for technology and growth equities. When rate expectations are in flux, long-duration assets suffer from both numerator and denominator pressure: earnings revisions may flatten, while discount rates rise, compressing valuation multiples. This week’s broad-based de-rating of software, cybersecurity, and high-beta AI names is a textbook example of such dynamic. Names with more visible near-term profitability, stronger free cash flow margins, and less reliance on long-dated terminal value—such as Arm, Marvell, and some of the more mature fintechs—tended to fare better, even when they sit in ostensibly similar thematic buckets. Investors continue to reward companies that can self-fund growth and show operating leverage, as these business models are less sensitive to swings in the cost of capital.

The macro environment is also influencing sector-level correlations and factor behavior. We are observing periods where traditional defensive sectors like healthcare and staples do not always provide the expected ballast, while certain cyclical groups trade more like defensives due to their cash flow profiles and return-of-capital frameworks. For example, UnitedHealth (UNH) fell 6.0% on the week and 8.9% on the month, underperforming many energy and materials names. Meanwhile, consumer-staples-like exposures such as Mondelez (MDLZ), which gained 3.7% this week, continue to provide some stability, but dispersion within consumer remains high, with names like Global-E (GLBE) and GoDaddy (GDDY) underperforming as more discretionary and long-duration e-commerce plays.

In this environment, macro and rates volatility amplify the importance of factor-aware portfolio construction. Traditional growth versus value classification no longer captures the nuances of how markets are pricing AI, energy, commodities, and digital business models. Instead, investors need to think in terms of duration of cash flows, balance sheet strength, exposure to real assets versus intangibles, and sensitivity to funding conditions. The moves this week underscore that even within growth, there is a spectrum—from hyper-growth, high-multiple names that are extremely sensitive to rates, to profitable, cash-generative franchises that can better withstand macro shocks. For the coming weeks, until there is greater clarity on the rate path and the macro trajectory, we expect this differentiation to remain a key driver of relative performance within our watchlist.

## Watchlist Deep Dives

### Braze (BRZE)

Braze was the standout outperformer on our watchlist, with a 25.5% gain over the week and 30.8% over the month, bucking the broader downtrend in software and adtech-oriented names. The company sits at the intersection of customer engagement, marketing automation, and first-party data, which are increasingly strategic capabilities for brands navigating privacy shifts and the decline of third-party cookies. The market’s enthusiasm reflects a growing recognition that Braze’s real-time customer engagement platform can benefit from AI-driven personalization and campaign optimization, enhancing both the value proposition to customers and the potential for operating leverage as scale increases.

The magnitude of the move suggests that both fundamental buyers and technical factors are at play. Following a strong prior earnings print and constructive guidance, incremental upgrades or target price increases likely contributed to renewed interest in the stock, while crowded shorts or underweight positions may have been forced to re-balance into strength. In an otherwise challenging week for software, Braze’s outperformance also highlights the value of being positioned in names with clear, near-term monetization of AI and data capabilities, rather than purely aspirational AI narratives. That said, with a 30.8% monthly gain, investors should be mindful of valuation risk and the potential for volatility if growth decelerates or marketing budgets tighten in a slower macro environment.

### Coinbase (COIN)

Coinbase’s 18.4% weekly decline and 12.4% monthly drawdown illustrate the heightened beta and sentiment sensitivity inherent in crypto-exposed financials. The company’s fundamentals are heavily tied to crypto trading volumes, asset price levels, and the evolving regulatory landscape, all of which tend to be highly volatile. In weeks where macro uncertainty is elevated and risk appetite diminishes, COIN often finds itself at the center of de-risking, as investors seek to reduce exposure to the most volatile corners of their portfolios. The combination of sector-specific regulatory risks and broader risk-off dynamics made Coinbase one of the most vulnerable names on our watchlist this week.

From a fundamental perspective, long-term investors remain focused on Coinbase’s ability to diversify revenue streams beyond transaction fees into recurring subscriptions, custody, institutional services, and on-chain revenue opportunities. However, the path to a more resilient and less cyclically sensitive business model is likely to be gradual, and near-term earnings will continue to ebb and flow with market conditions in digital assets. For portfolio managers, the current setup argues for a cautious, tactical approach to COIN exposure, treating it as a high-beta expression of crypto sentiment rather than a core holding unless there is unusual conviction about the regulatory and adoption trajectory.

### Micron Technology (MU)

Micron’s 15.5% weekly decline and 16.7% monthly drawdown underscore the cyclical and sentiment-driven nature of the memory business, even in an era where AI and data proliferation are creating structurally higher demand for advanced memory technologies. Investors have become increasingly concerned about where the industry sits in the memory cycle, worrying that recent pricing strength and AI-related demand could give way to increased supply, inventory builds, or a pause in hyperscaler spending. The weakness in SanDisk (SNDK), down 13.2% for the week, and Seagate (STX), down 7.6%, further reinforces the idea that storage broadly is undergoing a period of multiple compression.

That said, long-term demand drivers for high-bandwidth memory, SSDs, and advanced storage solutions remain compelling. AI training and inference workloads are memory-intensive, and advanced node transitions continue to support content increases per device. For Micron, the challenge is less about structural demand and more about navigating short-term supply-demand imbalances while executing on cost downs and technology transitions. The recent pullback may offer a better long-term entry point, but given the cyclicality, investors should be prepared for continued volatility and consider pairing MU with more structurally defensive or IP-driven semi names like Arm or Marvell.

### Tenable (TENB) and Rapid7 (RPD)

Tenable and Rapid7, both down roughly 16.5–16.6% on the week and around 13–16% on the month, were among the hardest-hit cybersecurity names and some of the largest decliners in the entire watchlist. Both are positioned in vulnerability management and security analytics, areas that are strategically important but also highly competitive and exposed to budget scrutiny. The scale of this week’s move, in the absence of fresh earnings or major company-specific news, suggests that these names have been caught in a broader de-risking of mid-cap, higher-growth cybersecurity, which had been a popular way to play secular security demand.

As investors reassess positioning, the key questions for Tenable and Rapid7 are whether their paths to profitability and free cash flow generation are sufficiently clear, and whether they can maintain differentiation against larger platform vendors that are increasingly bundling vulnerability and analytics functionality. The recent drawdowns may create opportunities for investors comfortable with elevated volatility and willing to underwrite multi-year growth in security spending, but they also highlight the benefit of tilting exposure toward better-capitalized, more profitable platforms like Palo Alto Networks or CrowdStrike when macro and rate uncertainty are high.

### Zscaler (ZS), SentinelOne (S), and CrowdStrike (CRWD)

Zscaler’s 12.1% weekly decline, SentinelOne’s 11.2% drop, and CrowdStrike’s 9.6% decline capture the broad risk-off move in security, but also illustrate nuances within the sector. All three are closely associated with high-growth, cloud-native security, zero trust, and endpoint/XDR—areas of persistent secular demand and key components of modern security architectures. Investors had rewarded these franchises with premium multiples based on high net retention, rapid ARR growth, and strong competitive positions. This week’s selloff is better understood as valuation compression in response to macro and rates uncertainty than a shift in the underlying security demand picture.

The longer-term investment cases for Zscaler, SentinelOne, and CrowdStrike remain grounded in the ongoing transition toward cloud-delivered security, consolidation of point solutions into platforms, and the integration of AI into threat detection and response. For Zscaler, secure access and zero trust network architectures are still early in penetration; for CrowdStrike, its Falcon platform continues to expand across modules and use cases; and for SentinelOne, the focus is on improving operating leverage and scaling profitably. The recent pullbacks may provide an opportunity to incrementally add to high-conviction names on weakness, but investors should remain selective and conscious of the elevated volatility that can accompany premium-multiple stocks in a risk-off tape.

### MongoDB (MDB), Snowflake (SNOW), and Elastic (ESTC)

MongoDB, down 9.8% for the week and 25.2% for the month, Snowflake, down 9.1% for the week and 9.7% for the month, and Elastic, down 9.0% for the week and 16.3% for the month, represent the core of our modern data platform cohort. These companies are fundamental building blocks for cloud-native applications, analytics, and, increasingly, AI workloads. However, they share common characteristics that make them vulnerable in a risk-off, rate-sensitive environment: high growth, premium valuations, and earnings stories that are still more about long-term TAM and platform expansion than near-term profitability.

Investors are now recalibrating how much AI-driven upside to embed in the near- and medium-term forecasts for these platforms. While their architectures position them well to benefit from AI—through vector search, real-time analytics, and scalable data storage and processing—the revenue and margin impacts will likely be gradual rather than immediate. The recent compression in multiples across this group is therefore a function of expectations normalizing from very elevated levels, rather than a deterioration in underlying fundamentals. For long-term oriented portfolios, these names continue to represent core enablers of the AI and cloud data stack, but exposure should be sized with an awareness of the volatility inherent in their current stage of maturity.

### Arm Holdings (ARM) and Marvell Technology (MRVL)

Arm’s 8.9% weekly gain and 9.4% monthly increase, along with Marvell’s 7.9% weekly and 17.2% monthly gains, highlight investor preference for IP-rich, AI-levered semiconductor stories. Arm’s licensing and royalty business model provides asset-light exposure to the proliferation of Arm-based designs across mobile, data center, automotive, and edge devices. As demand for custom AI accelerators, specialized inference chips, and energy-efficient compute grows, Arm is positioned to capture a rising share of silicon value without bearing the capital intensity of manufacturing.

Marvell, on the other hand, offers a more direct play on AI infrastructure, with exposure to custom ASICs for large customers, high-speed networking, storage controllers, and data center interconnects. Its recent stock performance reflects increasing investor conviction that AI-related demand will sustain elevated growth in its core segments, even as other parts of the semiconductor complex face cyclical pressures. For portfolios seeking AI exposure with a more tangible revenue and margin bridge than some software or speculative AI plays, Arm and Marvell present compelling options, though valuation discipline remains important after their recent runs.

### Sable Offshore (SOC) and Energy Complex

Sable Offshore’s 13.3% weekly and 102.1% monthly gains make it one of the most dramatic movers across the entire watchlist, underscoring both the leverage and the risk embedded in offshore energy names. The stock’s performance reflects a confluence of factors: structurally tighter offshore supply, improving project economics, and increased investor interest in names that can benefit from a multi-year upcycle in offshore development. The magnitude of the move raises the probability that some of the recent upside has been amplified by short covering and momentum-driven flows, which can reverse quickly if commodity prices or sentiment weaken.

Other energy names also delivered strong performance. Occidental Petroleum gained 7.6% this week and 28.2% over the month, Devon Energy rose 7.0% on the week and 22.2% on the month, California Resources gained 8.3% weekly and 18.5% monthly, and Valero added 6.0% for the week and 27.4% for the month. These moves reflect market confidence in the cash generation and disciplined capital return policies of these companies, as well as their role as partial hedges against inflation and geopolitical risk. For diversified portfolios that have been underweight energy, the recent outperformance raises the question of whether to chase strength or wait for more attractive entry points, particularly given the inherent volatility of commodity-linked equities.

### CF Industries (CF), Eastman Chemical (EMN), and Materials

CF Industries, up 9.2% for the week and 41.9% for the month, sits at the intersection of agriculture, energy, and industrials, and has emerged as a major beneficiary of renewed investor interest in the materials complex. The company’s nitrogen fertilizer business is leveraged to both agricultural demand and natural gas spreads, and its strong recent performance suggests expectations for robust cash generation in the coming quarters. Eastman Chemical (EMN), with a 9.0% weekly gain despite a 5.7% monthly decline, has likely benefited from short covering and some reassessment of its positioning in specialty materials, which can serve as critical inputs for a wide range of industrial and consumer applications.

Agnico Eagle and Newmont (NEM), up 8.0% and 6.6% this week but down roughly 18–20% over the month, highlight the volatility within precious metals equities, where sentiment can shift rapidly in response to changes in risk appetite, real yields, and currency dynamics. Freeport-McMoRan, up 8.0% for the week and down 18.3% for the month, underscores a similar pattern in copper, where long-term electrification and infrastructure demand remain supportive, but near-term concerns about global growth and Chinese demand have weighed on valuations. For investors looking to balance technology and growth exposure with real asset and commodity plays, this week’s materials performance provides a reminder of both the diversification benefits and the risk inherent in these sectors.

### Fastly (FSLY) and Cloud Infrastructure

Fastly’s 8.8% weekly and 51.1% monthly gains stand out against a backdrop of weakness in many other cloud infrastructure and software names. The company, which provides edge cloud and content delivery services, appears to be benefitting from both company-specific execution improvements and a broader re-rating of edge computing as a critical component of modern application delivery. Its strong performance suggests that investors are warming to turnaround and underdog narratives where there is a credible path to improved growth and profitability.

In contrast, other infrastructure names experienced more muted or negative performance. Cloudflare (NET) declined 5.8% for the week but remains up 18.2% for the month, reflecting its positioning as a core beneficiary of secure, programmable network services and security at the edge. Everpure (PSTG), down 5.8% for the week and 19.8% for the month, highlights investor concerns about storage and hybrid cloud demand. Arista Networks (ANET), down 8.0% this week and 9.1% over the month, has also given back some of its prior AI-fueled gains, though it remains a key player in high-speed data center networking.

### ServiceNow (NOW), Atlassian (TEAM), and Workday (WDAY)

Within large-cap enterprise software, ServiceNow’s 9.9% weekly decline, Atlassian’s 11.7% drop, and Workday’s 8.7% decline underscore the market’s willingness to de-rate even high-quality, mission-critical software platforms when macro and rates uncertainty rises. These companies have strong competitive positions, high net retention rates, and significant opportunities to expand through new modules, AI-enhanced workflows, and international growth. However, they also trade at premium valuations relative to the broader market, making them vulnerable to multiple compression during risk-off periods.

For ServiceNow, the long-term thesis centers on its role as a workflow automation and platform-of-platforms provider, increasingly embedding AI into IT, employee, and customer workflows. Atlassian remains key to developer collaboration and agile planning, and Workday is integral to HR and financial management for large enterprises. None of these theses have fundamentally changed over the past week; rather, the drawdowns create a more attractive risk-reward for long-term investors, provided they can tolerate near-term volatility and the absence of immediate earnings catalysts.

### Hims & Hers (HIMS) and Consumer-Adjacent Tech

Hims & Hers, down 12.0% on the week but still up 22.5% on the month, offers a case study in the volatility of consumer-adjacent, DTC digital health names. The company has benefited from strong interest in telehealth, personalized wellness, and subscription-based care models, and recent performance suggests that investors are increasingly open to the story. However, with a 22.5% monthly gain, some profit taking and factor-driven de-risking were almost inevitable during a week when broader risk appetite diminished.

The key questions for HIMS revolve around unit economics, customer acquisition costs, churn, and the sustainability of growth as competition intensifies and regulatory frameworks evolve. The weekly pullback should be viewed in the context of a still-strong monthly performance, indicating that while some momentum has been checked, the market has not fundamentally reversed its view on the name. Global-E’s 10.5% weekly and 17.6% monthly declines, and GoDaddy’s 5.8% weekly decline with a modest 1.1% monthly gain, reflect the challenges and opportunities in digital commerce and online infrastructure. ## Upcoming Catalysts

Within our watchlist, there are no earnings releases scheduled over the next fourteen days, which is unusual for periods of such elevated volatility but also instructive from a positioning standpoint. The lack of imminent company-specific catalysts implies that price action will be dominated by macro developments, sector rotation, and factor flows rather than discrete earnings surprises. For portfolio managers, this creates both risks and opportunities. On the one hand, stocks can move significantly on sentiment and flows alone, unmoored from changes in fundamental outlook. On the other hand, the absence of binary event risk allows for more flexible rebalancing, adding to high-conviction names on weakness and trimming exposure to crowded winners without the overhang of upcoming results.

Beyond earnings, several thematic catalysts remain relevant for the next few weeks and months. In AI infrastructure, ongoing announcements of new chips, partnerships, and large model deployments from hyperscalers and semiconductor companies will continue to shape sentiment around names like Arm, Marvell, Micron, and Arista Networks. For cybersecurity, any high-profile breaches, regulatory developments, or government spending initiatives can quickly alter the demand narrative and influence valuations across the sector. In fintech and digital assets, regulatory news, shifts in interest in crypto, and macro risk sentiment will remain key drivers for Coinbase, Block, and other payments names.

In energy and materials, commodity price movements and geopolitical developments will continue to act as primary catalysts for SOC, OXY, DVN, CRC, CF, AEM, FCX, and others. Investor focus will also be on how these companies articulate capital allocation priorities, including dividends, buybacks, and growth capex. In consumer and digital commerce, data points on consumer spending, promotional intensity, and cross-border trade can influence names like GLBE, GDDY, PVH, SHOP, and CLX. Finally, cross-asset signals from rates, credit spreads, and FX will inform overall risk appetite and the balance between growth and value within portfolios.

## What To Watch Next Week

Looking ahead to next week, the key challenge for investors in our watchlist will be navigating the intersection of macro uncertainty, factor rotation, and elevated single-stock volatility in the absence of major earnings events. The first order question is whether this week’s de-risking in software, cybersecurity, and select AI names marks the beginning of a more prolonged de-rating or a short, sharp positioning reset that could set the stage for a relief rally. Price and volume behavior early in the week, especially in liquid bellwethers such as Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, ServiceNow, CrowdStrike, and the core data platforms, will provide important clues as to whether selling pressure is abating or intensifying.

In software, we will be watching whether the IGV ETF and key constituents like ServiceNow, Atlassian, Workday, and HubSpot can stabilize after their 7–12% weekly declines. Any signs of stabilization, narrowing intraday ranges, and improved breadth would suggest that the worst of the mechanical de-risking may be behind us, creating an opportunity to selectively add to high-conviction names at more attractive valuations. Conversely, if weakness accelerates and spreads to more defensive software names, it would argue for a continued cautious stance and perhaps even further rotation into energy, materials, and industrials.

In cybersecurity, the focus will be on whether investors differentiate more clearly between platforms and niche players following this week’s indiscriminate selling. Watch how Tenable, Rapid7, Zscaler, SentinelOne, Qualys, Varonis, Palo Alto Networks, and CrowdStrike trade relative to each other. Outperformance of larger, more profitable platforms would indicate a quality rotation within the sector, while continued broad selling could signal that positioning is still too crowded. Any incremental news flow on security incidents or budget trends will also be important inputs.

For semiconductors and AI infrastructure, we will monitor whether the bifurcation persists between AI-levered IP names like Arm and Marvell and more cyclical players like Micron, SanDisk, Seagate, and Credo. If AI-related names continue to outperform while cyclicals lag, it will reinforce the narrative that investors are willing to own AI-enablers with more visible growth and margin trajectories, even at higher multiples. However, if we see a broad-based rebound in semis, it could suggest that the recent weakness was mostly a macro scare rather than a change in the industry outlook.

In energy and materials, the key question is whether the strong performance of SOC, OXY, DVN, CRC, CF, EMN, AEM, FCX, CNH, and others can sustain in the face of any moderation in commodity prices or a shift in macro sentiment. We will watch for signs of exhaustion in these trades, such as intraday reversals from new highs or increasing negative reactions to positive news, which would suggest that a near-term consolidation or pullback may be ahead. At the same time, given their strong cash flow generation and capital return potential, these sectors will remain central to discussions about portfolio barbell strategies.

Across fintech, consumer, and digital commerce, we will follow whether names like Coinbase, Block, Bill, Global Payments, Global-E, GoDaddy, PVH, Mondelez, and Unilever continue to trade primarily as macro and factor proxies or begin to decouple based on idiosyncratic factors. For Coinbase in particular, next week’s price action will indicate whether this week’s 18.4% decline has fully reset expectations or whether there is more downside pressure as investors continue to cut risk. Similarly, the persistence of Braze’s 25.5% weekly gain—or lack thereof—will shed light on how sticky the recent re-rating is for high-growth MarTech names in a volatile tape.

From a portfolio strategy perspective, next week is likely to be about incremental adjustments rather than wholesale reorientation. The priority should be to reassess position sizes in names that have moved sharply—both winners and losers—to ensure that exposures remain aligned with conviction levels and risk tolerance. For high-quality secular winners that have sold off without fundamental deterioration, such as core SaaS platforms, data infrastructure names, and leading cybersecurity franchises, this may be an opportunity to gradually build positions. For cyclicals and commodities that have rallied strongly, such as SOC, CF, OXY, and DVN, the focus should be on managing gains and guarding against potential reversals while still recognizing their role as hedges and diversifiers.

In sum, the week ahead will test whether the market’s recent rotation away from long-duration growth and AI beneficiaries toward energy, materials, and cyclicals has further to run or is nearing exhaustion. With no watchlist earnings catalysts to provide fresh fundamental information, investors must rely on price action, macro developments, and relative performance signals to navigate this environment. Maintaining flexibility, emphasizing balance between growth and value, and focusing on quality within each sector remain the guiding principles for managing risk and capturing opportunities in the current phase of the cycle.

risks.impact: Shifts in expectations for growth, inflation, and central bank policy remain the dominant macro risk for US equities. A more persistent higher-for-longer rate regime would disproportionately pressure long-duration growth assets such as software and hyperscalers, where earnings are further out in time. Conversely, any sign of softer activity could challenge the nascent rotation into cyclicals and commodities. Investors should watch upcoming inflation prints, policy communication, and rate-volatility metrics for clues on factor performance and equity risk premia repricing in the coming weeks and months. Higher real yields would likely extend the current de-grossing in crowded tech leadership, while a stabilisation in yields could allow for a selective re-risking into quality growth at more attractive entry points. Positioning data and ETF flows will be important to gauge whether recent selling has been largely mechanical or reflects a deeper shift in fundamental conviction. An abrupt move in rates either way could produce further cross-asset volatility and amplify factor rotations, affecting portfolio construction and risk budgeting across strategies. Monitoring credit spreads alongside rates will also help assess whether macro stress is creeping into broader financial conditions or remains contained within rate-sensitive growth pockets. Stable credit and modest rate moves would favour a more benign environment for stock picking, while a simultaneous widening could trigger a broader de-risking wave across equities. Vol-targeting and risk-parity strategies may adjust exposures rapidly to rate volatility, adding an additional mechanical layer to equity market moves that investors need to anticipate and incorporate into scenario planning. Rising funding costs could also pressure smaller, unprofitable companies and structurally change the opportunity set in certain high-growth sectors over time. In this environment, capital allocation discipline and balance sheet strength are likely to be increasingly rewarded by the market and should be key selection criteria for new investments and add-on trades in existing positions. Traders should remain alert to sharp intraday moves around data releases and consider using options to hedge nonlinear rate-shock scenarios that are difficult to manage with linear exposures alone. They should also revisit stop-loss and gross/net exposure frameworks to ensure portfolios can withstand swings in rates without forced selling at the worst points of volatility. A patient, staged approach to adding risk after macro events may prove more resilient than attempting to time the exact inflection in rate expectations or factor performance. Over the medium term, the interplay between rates, inflation, and productivity expectations from AI will shape the relative attractiveness of growth versus value and the overall equity risk premium. Maintaining flexibility and multiple contingency plans for divergent macro paths is essential in this phase of the cycle, especially given the potential for policy missteps or data revisions to abruptly change consensus narratives. Investors should also be wary of overfitting to the most recent macro regime and remain open to the possibility that correlations and factor behaviors may differ from prior cycles as structural forces, including demographics and technology, evolve.

risks.impact: The heavy concentration of market leadership in a narrow cohort of tech and AI beneficiaries leaves indices vulnerable to a more prolonged de-grossing in the space. With META, GOOG, and MSFT all down materially on the week, and software infrastructure and application names such as SNOW, MDB, NOW, and TEAM also under pressure, the risk is that risk managers force further de-risking if volatility remains elevated. This could trigger a feedback loop where ETF and options flows exacerbate underlying fundamental concerns, at least in the short term. Investors should monitor breadth metrics, large-cap tech correlation, and flows into sector and factor ETFs to assess whether the selling is becoming indiscriminate. A more durable correction in AI-exposed names could temporarily cap index-level upside even if underlying economic data remain constructive, as benchmark-heavy weights drag on performance. However, such a correction could also create more attractive entry points into high-quality franchises with durable moats and long runways, provided earnings revisions hold up. Differentiating between companies whose AI narratives are backed by tangible monetisation and those still in proof-of-concept stages will be key to risk management and alpha generation. In addition, sustained volatility in mega-cap tech can distort intra-day market microstructure, impacting liquidity and execution conditions across the broader market. Portfolio managers may need to adjust exposure and hedging frameworks to account for this, potentially increasing the use of index-level options or dispersion strategies. Over time, a more balanced leadership structure outside a narrow tech cohort could reduce tail risk at the index level but also change the character of returns and correlations that many quantitative strategies rely on. This transition period may be bumpy and requires enhanced monitoring of factor behaviour, crowding indicators, and single-name event risk. Failure to adjust to these shifting dynamics could leave portfolios inadvertently overexposed to common risk factors despite appearing diversified at the sector level.

In software and cybersecurity, investors are already attuned to signs of deal elongation, seat optimization, and increased budget scrutiny, which could lead to guidance resets for names like CRWD, PANW, ZS, and HUBS if macro conditions soften. Similarly, semiconductors face the dual challenge of navigating AI-driven demand against cyclical inventory corrections in areas such as memory and storage, with companies like MU and WDC particularly exposed. Investors should pay close attention to high-frequency indicators from channel checks, third-party data, and early reporters in each supply chain to gauge whether fundamental trends are deteriorating ahead of consensus. A rolling guidance cut cycle could prompt further multiple compression and a more sustained rotation into value, cyclicals, and income-generating assets. Conversely, resilience in earnings and guidance relative to expectations could help stabilise sentiment and set a floor under high-quality growth, especially if valuations reset to more defensible levels. The absence of near-term watchlist earnings reduces imminent single-name event risk but also concentrates focus on macro data and any unscheduled corporate updates, which could increase the surprise factor of negative or positive pre-announcements. For active managers, this environment underscores the importance of rigorous bottom-up work and differentiated views on company-specific earnings power rather than relying solely on top-down factor or thematic exposure.

Conversely, resilience in earnings and guidance relative to expectations could help stabilise sentiment and set a floor under high-quality growth, especially if valuations reset to more defensible levels. risks.risk: Regulatory and policy uncertainty in fintech and crypto
risks.impact: Fintech and crypto-adjacent assets are facing ongoing regulatory and policy scrutiny, which adds an additional layer of risk beyond traditional macro and rate considerations. COIN’s sharp weekly decline illustrates how sensitive market pricing is to shifting expectations around enforcement actions, rule making, and policy statements, especially in the absence of clear, stable frameworks. Broader fintech platforms such as FOUR, BILL, and XYZ are also exposed to evolving regulatory standards in areas such as payments, consumer protection, and data privacy, which could impact growth trajectories and compliance costs. Policy developments can arrive abruptly and outside of the normal macro data calendar, meaning headline risk is elevated and more difficult to hedge systematically. Investors should monitor legislative developments, enforcement news, and cross-border regulatory coordination, particularly between US and international bodies, to assess the direction of travel. Unfavourable outcomes could structurally reduce addressable markets or introduce new frictions in customer acquisition and product rollout. Conversely, the gradual emergence of clearer rules could de-risk the space and unlock fresh institutional participation over time, particularly for platforms with strong governance and compliance cultures. The near term, however, is likely to remain volatile and headline-driven, favouring nimble positioning, careful position sizing, and the selective use of options to manage gap risk around major policy events or court decisions. In addition, higher funding costs and macro uncertainty could intersect with regulatory pressure to create a more challenging operating environment for less diversified or less capitalised fintech firms. Investors may need to differentiate more sharply between those with robust balance sheets and durable competitive advantages versus those reliant on aggressive growth to justify valuations.

risks.impact: An environment of elevated volatility and rapid factor rotations increases the risk that underlying market structure and liquidity conditions become a source of instability. The heavy presence of options-driven strategies, systematic volatility-targeting funds, and ETFs concentrating flows into and out of narrow cohorts of names can amplify price moves, as seen in the sharp swings across software, semis, and select high-beta growth names. If liquidity were to thin materially, especially during macro events or into low-volume periods, relatively small order imbalances could produce outsized price gaps and dislocations in both directions. This is particularly relevant for mid-cap software, cybersecurity, and niche tech names such as TENB, RPD, ZETA, and POET, where market depth can be limited relative to the scale of institutional flows. Investors should pay attention to bid-ask spreads, depth-of-book metrics, and intraday volatility patterns as early warning signs of deteriorating liquidity conditions. In challenging tapes, it may be prudent to adjust execution strategies, including using limit orders more frequently, staggering large trades over time, or leveraging dark pools appropriately while remaining mindful of information leakage. A significant liquidity shock could also impact index-level products and derivatives, leading to a temporary decoupling between underlying fundamentals and market pricing. For portfolio managers, this underscores the importance of stress testing positions against gaps in less-liquid names and ensuring that overall portfolio construction allows for orderly risk reduction if conditions worsen. Over the longer term, persistent liquidity challenges could change how capital is allocated across sectors, favouring larger, more liquid names and potentially raising the cost of capital for smaller, fast-growing companies.

market_summary: US equities saw a sharp factor reversal as crowded growth, software, and AI leadership sold off while energy, materials, and select industrials outperformed. High-beta tech under pressure included hyperscalers like META and GOOG and software platforms such as TEAM, NOW, and HUBS, while semis were mixed with MU weak but ARM and MRVL resilient. Rotation favored commodity and energy exposure, with CF, VLO, OXY, DVN, and copper levered FCX all posting strong weekly gains, alongside specialty materials GLW and EMN. Into the coming weeks, positioning remains fragile with software multiples compressing, cyclicals gaining incremental sponsorship, and macro data plus rates trajectory likely dictating whether this is a deeper de-grossing or a buyable shakeout in high-quality growth.
